opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so budget forcing came out of our work on s1, where we were asking: what's the simplest possible way to get test-time scaling? The idea is really minimal. We intervene directly on the decoding process at inference time, with no extra training and no fancy search.

There are two directions. If you want the model to think less, you enforce a maximum number of thinking tokens. Once the model hits that budget, you append the end-of-thinking delimiter, and maybe something like "Final Answer:", which forces it to stop reasoning and commit to an answer based on what it has so far.

The more interesting direction is making the model think longer. When the model tries to end its reasoning, we suppress the end-of-thinking token and append the word "Wait" to its reasoning trace instead. That nudges the model to keep going, and often it reconsiders its previous steps. We saw cases where it had made a mistake, then after "Wait" it double-checked and corrected itself. You can do that repeatedly, appending "Wait" two, four, or six times, and performance on benchmarks like AIME goes up as you extend the thinking.

We compared it against other ways of controlling length. One was conditioning on the length in the prompt, like telling the model "think for this many tokens" or "this many steps." Another was rejection sampling, where you sample until you get a response that fits the budget. Budget forcing gave the best combination of control, meaning you actually hit the budget you want, and scaling, meaning more compute reliably translates into better accuracy.

It's not unlimited, though. If you keep forcing it, performance eventually flattens out. The model can start repeating itself or getting stuck in loops, and the context window is a hard limit too. But what I found exciting is that with just around a thousand carefully curated training examples and this one simple trick, you get a clear test-time scaling curve. It suggests a lot of the reasoning ability is already in the base model. You mostly have to unlock it and give it room to think.

r001.rationale: It says to enforce a maximum thinking-token budget and, once reached, append the end-of-thinking delimiter to stop reasoning and produce an answer.

r002.rationale: It says to suppress the end-of-thinking token and append “Wait” to the reasoning trace when the model tries to stop, prompting it to continue.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so budget forcing is actually a really simple idea, which is kind of what we liked about it. The context is that we had this model, s1, which we'd fine-tuned on just a thousand carefully selected reasoning examples, and the question was: can we get test-time scaling behavior out of it, where if you let it think longer, it does better? And the problem is that the model, on its own, decides when to stop thinking. It writes its chain of thought, emits an end-of-thinking token, and then gives you the answer. So we don't really have a knob.

Budget forcing is just intervening on that at decode time. There are two directions. If we want to cap the compute, we set a maximum number of thinking tokens, and when the model hits that limit, we forcibly append the end-of-thinking delimiter, and often something like "Final Answer:", so the model is forced to transition out of reasoning and commit to an answer with whatever it's got. That's the lower end of the scaling curve.

The more interesting direction is forcing it to think more. When the model tries to emit the end-of-thinking token and we want more compute, we suppress that token and instead append the string "Wait" to its reasoning trace. And what happens is the model reads "Wait" and treats it as a cue to reconsider, so it goes back and double-checks its work, catches arithmetic errors, tries a different approach. We can do this once, twice, several times, and each time you get a longer trace and generally a better answer. On AIME, for example, extrapolating like this took the model from something like fifty to around fifty-seven percent.

We did try alternatives. We tried different strings — "Alternatively," "Hmm," just the end-of-thinking token with nothing — and "Wait" worked best. We also compared against things like conditional control, where you train the model to respect a budget stated in the prompt, or rejection sampling on length. Those were either less controllable or, in the case of rejection sampling, actually inverted the scaling — shorter samples tended to be the ones where the model was confident and correct. Budget forcing gave us perfect controllability by construction and the best scaling slope.

The honest caveat is that it does flatten out eventually. If you append "Wait" too many times, the model starts looping, repeating the same checks, and you run into the context window. So it's not infinite scaling, it's a way of extracting and measuring the scaling that's in the model. But as a baseline, it's remarkable how far such a crude intervention gets you.

r001.rationale: It says a maximum number of thinking tokens is set, then the end-of-thinking delimiter is forcibly appended when that limit is reached.

r002.rationale: It explains that when the model tries to stop, the end-of-thinking token is suppressed and “Wait” is appended to the reasoning trace to prompt further thinking.

astra-6.text:
The idea behind budget forcing is to control how much the model thinks at inference time. If we want it to stop reasoning, we can insert the end-of-thinking token and have it produce an answer. If we want it to think longer, we suppress that token and append something like “Wait,” which encourages it to continue reasoning and potentially check its previous work.

So you can set a token budget and use those interventions to steer the amount of computation the model spends. Of course, thinking longer doesn’t guarantee a better answer—it might repeat itself or go down an unhelpful path—but it gives us a simple way to explore that tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response mentions setting a token budget and steering computation, but does not explain cutting off the reasoning trace when that budget is reached.

r002.rationale: It explains suppressing the end-of-thinking token and appending “Wait” to encourage the model to continue reasoning past its stopping point.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea behind budget forcing was to control the amount of thinking at inference time without having to retrain the model for each budget. We did that in two ways. If we wanted the model to reason less, we could cut off its thinking by inserting the end-of-thinking token and have it produce an answer. If we wanted it to reason longer, we could suppress that token and append “Wait,” which encouraged it to continue thinking—to check its work or consider another approach.

What was interesting was that this very simple intervention could improve accuracy. The model might initially have an incorrect answer, but with that extra opportunity to think, it could catch its mistake. Of course, more thinking doesn’t guarantee a better answer every time, but it gave us a straightforward way to study how performance changes as you allocate more inference-time compute.

r001.rationale: The response says to cut off the model’s thinking by inserting the end-of-thinking token, but does not specify cutting it off at a token budget.

r002.rationale: The response says to suppress the stopping token and append “Wait,” encouraging the model to continue thinking.
